title: Argumentation for explainable scheduling
contribution: Defines ArgOpt, which maps makespan schedules to abstract-argumentation frameworks whose stable extensions correspond exactly to feasible, efficient (SEP/PEP) or fixed-decision-respecting schedules, and extracts sound, complete, polynomial-time single-attack or non-attack explanations rendered as natural-language templates (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: Users see optimization solvers as unexplainable black boxes; nurse-rostering staff ask why a schedule is (not) feasible, efficient or consistent with their decisions; the need is stated as three formal desiderata: sound and complete, computationally tractable, cognitively tractable (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Assignments become arguments and feasibility conflicts become attacks, so stable extensions are feasible schedules; NP-hard optimality is replaced by the necessary exchange conditions SEP/PEP, encoded by editing attacks; fixed decisions become self-attacks or unattacked arguments; one attack or non-attack is the explanation (Defs 4.1-5.5, Thms 4.1-4.5, pp. 3-7).
assumptions: Makespan on identical parallel machines with m, n > 1; efficiency = feasibility + SEP + PEP, explicitly not optimality, because explaining optimality in polynomial time is ruled out unless P=NP; fixed decisions must be compatible (pp. 2-3).
proof_devices: Iff correspondence theorem by contradiction on sum_i x_ij > 1 (conflict) or = 0 (unattacked argument) (Thm 4.1, p. 4)
Exchange argument showing single and pairwise exchange properties are necessary for optimality (Lemma 3.2, p. 3)
Attack-editing invariance: SEP/PEP and fixed-decision edits preserve conflict-freeness/stability of the feasibility AF (Thms 4.3, 4.5, pp. 5-6)
Adjacency-list complexity lemmas: O(nm^2) construction, O(n^2 m^2) stability check (Lemmas 4.2, 4.4, 4.6, pp. 5-6)
Assembly theorem for soundness/completeness and polynomial time/size (Thm 5.1, p. 8)
experiments: none: no computational or user study; toy examples with 2 machines and 2-3 jobs (Examples 4.3-5.8, pp. 5-7); 'No new data was collected' (p. 8).
positioning: Claims no prior work on explainable scheduling or on argumentation explaining optimization; separates from explainable planning, multicriteria argumentation, abduction for scheduling and optimization-implemented argumentation solvers; contrasts length-1 explanations with chain-style argumentative explanations; defers ML-explanation comparison (p. 8).
writing: Named paradigm (ArgOpt) with a page-1 layer figure; 'What makes an optimization solution good?' framing; definition-lemma-theorem-example cadence with one running nurse example; NLG templates printed verbatim; modest 'first steps' claim (pp. 1, 7).
limits_future: Only makespan on identical machines and only necessary conditions; cognitive tractability proved as polynomial size, not user-tested; future: contractual constraints, robustness to uncertainty, explanations of fractional relaxations or cutting planes, comparison with ML explanations (pp. 3, 8).

method_links.note: MILP structure (assignment constraint alone determines feasibility) is re-represented as an argumentation graph, but for human explanation rather than a stronger relaxation; no detector validation.
Outside the solver-paper genre: no benchmark at all, toy instances only; the audit standard does not travel to this co-authored AI-venue theory paper.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Optimality explanation is NP-hard, so the paper certifies and explains violations of single/pairwise exchange conditions instead and says so explicitly.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization brought into a neighbouring AI formalism
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Abstract argumentation used as an intermediate layer between solver and user (ArgOpt); argumentation group leads, optimization side supplies model and optimality conditions.

transferable: Replace an NP-hard certificate (optimality) by polynomially checkable necessary conditions and explain violations of those (pp. 3, 5).
State explanation desiderata formally (sound/complete, polynomial time, polynomial size) and discharge them in one theorem (pp. 3, 8).
Give every encoding theorem a companion construction/verification complexity lemma (pp. 5-6).
coauthors: Kristijonas Cyras (first), Dimitrios Letsios, Francesca Toni (Imperial College London)

quotes.text: We have restricted attention to feasible and efficient (rather than optimal) solutions because answering and explaining why an arbitrary schedule is optimal in polynomial time is ruled out due to NP-hardness of makespan scheduling, unless P=NP.
SEP and PEP are necessary optimality conditions (but not sufficient; see e.g. the list-scheduling algorithm tightness analysis in (Williamson and Shmoys 2011)).

title: Scoring positive semidefinite cutting planes for quadratic optimization via trained neural networks
contribution: Outer-approximates the QP semidefinite relaxation with sparse low-dimensional eigenvalue cuts selected by expected objective improvement, estimated by instance-independent offline-trained neural networks and combined with a feasibility measure for convergence, closing most of the McCormick-to-SDP gap on all 99 BoxQP instances and complementing triangle/BGL relaxations at low overhead (Nov 2019 preprint read).
problem_entry: Global solvers built on polyhedral relaxations cannot exploit SDP strength; four solver-integration desiderata (easy integration, light, few cuts, convergence); existing cut selection is feasibility-based and objective selection needs prohibitively many small SDPs (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Decompose the PSD constraint into n-dimensional principal-submatrix cones (n <= 5) over sparsity-based covers, rank candidate eigenvalue cuts by objective improvement of a fixed-x rho-subproblem, replace that SDP by a trained NN estimator, and combine with violation via C(rho) (pp. 5-12, 15, 24-25).
assumptions: QP over [0,1]^N with linear constraints and indefinite Q; no disconnected vertex in the sparsity graph; X_ii <= x_i to bound SDP; fixing x at LP solution guarantees PSD completion and cut validity; inputs rescaled to eigenvalues in [-1,1] using linearity in Q; training sampled by spectrum (pp. 3-4, 10, 14-15).
proof_devices: Chordal decomposition with an added universal vertex v so x enters every clique; bound of S^E_n equals S at clique number (Lemma 3.1.2, pp. 6-7)
Hierarchy S_2 contains S_3 ... contains S via PSD principal minors (Remark 3.1.4, p. 7)

Separation-theorem outer-approximation in one direction; restrictiveness grows with extra constraints or larger fixing, later used to explain observations (o4)-(o6), (o9) (Lemma 3.2.3, p. 9; App. A.1, p. 35)
Optimality-based bound z^L_qp <= z_qp explaining weaker final optimality-selection bounds (Corollary 3.2.4, p. 10; App. A.2, pp. 35-36)
Eigenvalue-to-entry bound for input scaling (Lemma 4.1.1, p. 15)
experiments: NN: 1M samples (75/15/10), tanh+SCG, 3-4 layers, 0.5M test fits (Fig. 7, p. 17; App. A.3, p. 36); NN 1-2 orders faster than Mosek/SeDuMi (Table 2, p. 18); Algorithm 1 cut loop (20 rounds, 0.1% stop) on all 99 BoxQP by size/density with random control (Tables 3-8, Figs 8-12, pp. 19-30); mixing with triangle inequalities vs BGL as CPLEX-relaxation proxy (Table 9, Figs 13-14, pp. 31-33); 320 QCQP results on GitHub (p. 33); single-thread AWS; no full branch-and-cut runs.
positioning: Builds on Qualizza-Belotti-Margot and Sherali-style eigen cuts, answers Dey-Molinaro's hint to use ML in cut selection, borrows deep objective cuts from Boyd-Vandenberghe; agrees ('echoes Qualizza et al.') and disagrees ('contrary to [94, 105]') openly; places multiterm/edge-concave relaxations as complements (pp. 3, 8-9, 26, 29).
writing: Numbered desiderata on p. 2 closed one by one in the conclusion; numbered observations (o1)-(o10) each tied to a lemma; summary trade-off Table 3; hedged 'Our hypothesis ... We claim, and attempt to show'; repeated two-part contribution sentence (pp. 2, 19-20, 34-35).
limits_future: No advantage on fully dense instances; estimator degrades with n; rank flips in late rounds; memory limits for jumbo high-density n=5; QCQP with little objective structure needs research; Lagrangian variant may not converge; future: copositive 3D, pooling cuts, orthogonality (pp. 20-22, 27, 29-30, 33, 35, 37).

method_links.note: Parameterised family S^E*_n from SOCP-type n=2 to the full SDP at clique number; sweep n in {3,4,5}; choice labelled 'heuristic guidelines'.
Exploits the sparsity-pattern graph and objective structure; prunes zero-coefficient subproblems (P*_3).
Designed for whole-solver integration and judged with other cut classes present (gap vanishes with triangle inequalities), but evidence stops at the root cut loop; no branch-and-cut runs.
Whole BoxQP set, random-selection control, commercial-relaxation proxy (BGL), loss on dense instances written in, per-instance results public.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: learned surrogate for an inner solve inside the solver
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Instance-independent NN trained offline replaces thousands of small SDP solves for cut scoring (ML for optimization, not optimization over ML); coauthored with CPLEX developers.

transferable: Train an instance-independent surrogate offline on a scaled canonical domain and rescale each instance's inputs to it via a linearity property (pp. 14-15).
Combine a learned score with an exact feasibility check and fall back to the exact rule once the learned rule does worse than random (Def. 5.2.1, pp. 24-25).
Sample matrix inputs by spectrum (random eigenvalues times Haar orthonormal basis), not entries (Table 1, p. 14).
Report gap closed per added cut and the false-positive share of selected cuts against a random-selection control (Figs 11-12, p. 25).
Prove one monotonicity lemma and cite it as the explanation of each numbered empirical observation (pp. 9, 26, 29).
coauthors: Radu Baltean-Lugojan (first, Imperial), Pierre Bonami and Andrea Tramontani (CPLEX Optimization, IBM)

quotes.text: An expensive approximation may be useful for a specific application, but general-purpose solvers cannot invest too much time in possibly unproductive cutting surfaces.
There is no advantage for using our proposed sparse cuts for fully-dense instances.

title: Robust optimization for the pooling problem
contribution: Applies duality-based robust reformulation and robust cutting planes (with an adaptive master-tolerance scheme for global solvers without callbacks) to the nonconvex pooling problem with uncertain inlet concentrations, compares them with an optimal safety-factor baseline over box, ellipsoidal and polyhedral sets on 14 instances, and shows how uncertainty changes the optimal network (arXiv v1 read).
problem_entry: Pooling has been treated deterministically and robust optimization has targeted convex or MILP problems; a four-category grid (convex/nonconvex outer x concave/nonconcave inner) shows pooling sits in the under-studied Category 2; multistage methods assume uncertainty is fully revealed (pp. 1-5).
key_idea: Because pooling is linear (concave) in every uncertain parameter and the q-formulation has no uncertain equalities, standard robust reformulations and cutting planes apply; couple cutting planes to ANTIGONE via a loosen-then-tighten master tolerance; benchmark against a minimal safety factor; build correlated ellipsoids from geography (pp. 7-15).
assumptions: Objective certain, constraints robustified one at a time; only inlet concentrations uncertain in p-norm sets of size r with deviation equal to nominal; single-stage; squared ellipsoid constraint needs the nominal constraint added (pp. 4, 9, 12, 15).
proof_devices: Strong-duality robust counterpart with per-geometry lambda terms (Table 1, eq. (14), pp. 6, 11)
Box set as worst-case coefficient shift, no complexity change (p. 12)
Model-size bookkeeping: ellipsoid O(|i||j|) with higher-order terms vs polyhedron O(|i||j||k|) but bilinear (p. 12)
Cutting-plane convergence from finitely many vertices (box/polyhedron) and Minguez-Casero-Alonso outer-approximation equivalence (ellipsoid) (pp. 13-14)
Safety factor shown equivalent to box uncertainty on quality bounds (p. 14)
experiments: GAMS 26.1.0, ANTIGONE 1.1 (NLP) and CPLEX 12.8 (MILP); 14 literature instances x 30 r values x 3 geometries; 1 h, 1e-6, <= 200 cuts (p. 15); flow diagrams and price-of-robustness curves (Figs 2-6, pp. 16-21); % solved and median time over solved only (Table 2, p. 20); 13.3 iterations on average (p. 18); correlation scenarios (Fig. 7, p. 22); single global solver.
positioning: Extends the authors' ESCAPE-29 paper; contrasts with Li-Misener-Floudas robust demand uncertainty and Barton/Li stochastic pooling; borrows Bertsimas-Dunning-Lubin's reformulation-vs-cutting-plane question from MILP; links cutting planes to control backoff (pp. 2-3, 7-8).
writing: Four contribution bullets; tutorial review of robust optimization for the I&EC audience; balanced verdict ('one important advantage'); hedged causal claims ('most likely due to'); no future-work paragraph (pp. 3-8, 18-20).
limits_future: Polyhedral set less conservative but maybe less robust; reformulation weak for ellipsoids; cutting-plane intermediates not robustly feasible; safety factor conservative; temporal/multistage effects and lazy-constraint integration left open (pp. 2, 7, 17-20).

method_links.note: A structural property (linearity in uncertain parameters; q-formulation without uncertain equalities) decides which robust methods apply and which formulation to use.
Verdict split by property rather than one winner: cutting planes solve more, reformulation yields feasible intermediates.
Standard literature set and disclosed unsolved runs, but only one (own) global solver, medians over solved instances only, no independent verification of returned points described.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: practitioner baseline calibrated to the rigorous answer
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Smallest safety factor that makes the nominal solution robustly feasible, found by bisection/secant search, used as both baseline and conservative approximation.

transferable: Adaptive master-problem tolerance to couple robust cutting planes with a global solver lacking lazy-constraint callbacks (Algorithm 1, p. 7).
Classify the problem in a convexity (outer) x concavity (inner) grid to show which method families apply (Fig. 1, p. 5).
Plot the price of robustness and mark where the optimal structure switches (Figs 2-3, pp. 16-17).
Construct correlated ellipsoidal uncertainty sets from a spatial kernel on source locations (eqs (10)-(11), p. 10).
coauthors: Johannes Wiebe (first, Imperial), Ines Cecilio (Schlumberger Cambridge Research)

quotes.text: Unlike mature MILP solver software, however, global optimization solvers do not routinely offer callbacks for adding lazy or incumbent constraints.
In contrast, intermediate solutions in the cutting plane algorithm are often not robustly feasible.

title: Symmetry detection for quadratic optimization using binary layered graphs
contribution: Represents a QCQP as a sparse coefficient tensor, converts it to an edge-labelled then binary-layered vertex-coloured graph that nauty can process to compute the formulation group, and uses symmetry knowledge to prune a grid approximation of point packing.
problem_entry: Symmetry makes branch-and-bound explore equivalent subtrees; detection exists for CP, IP and MINLP via expression DAGs; the paper offers an alternative representation for QCQP (pp. 1-3).
key_idea: Sparse tensor (M, I, J, K) -> edge-labelled vertex-coloured graph -> binary layered graph with ceil(log2(l+1)) layers encoding coefficient labels, fed to nauty; then orbit-based removal of reflected grid arrangements for point packing (pp. 3-9).
assumptions: Formulation group restricted to symmetry over the whole variable box because dom(f) may be nonconvex; finite bounds; grid approximation may miss the optimum (6 points: 0.5 vs 0.6009) (pp. 2-3, 8).
proof_devices: Reliance on isomorphism-preserving edge-label-to-layer transformation (McKay-Piperno) (p. 5)
Reliance on Liberti's map from graph automorphisms to the formulation group (p. 3)
Worked 4-variable example yielding G = (x1x4)(x2x3) (p. 7)
Pruning bound 1/(k*-1) on point separation (pp. 8-9)
experiments: One worked dreadnaut example and qualitative comparison with the DAG representation (p. 7); runtime of 2D symmetry removal for 6 points versus grid size and occupied grids (Fig. 11, p. 10); exhaustive-search results omitted; no instance library, no detection timings, no solver comparison.
positioning: Alternative to Liberti's expression-graph detection; tensor representation 'new to this paper'; places itself among Margot, Pfetsch-Rehn and application-specific symmetry handling; cites the group's own heat-exchanger symmetry and SUSPECT work (pp. 1, 3, 11-12).
writing: Short applied paper; abstract repeated at the end of the introduction; conclusion claims 'significantly better methods' beyond the single-instance evidence; CRediT-style contribution statement (pp. 1-2, 10).
limits_future: Grid can miss the optimum; DAG smaller on the example; symmetry-aware branch-and-bound not built; claimed advantage for many distinct coefficients unmeasured; relevance to industrial packing/nesting (pp. 7-10).

method_links.note: Symmetry stated as a graph a program (nauty) can match, then exploited (steps 3 and 6); SKILL.md already cites this DOI.
Step 5 missing: detector not validated against a labelled library, unlike SUSPECT's 1527-problem validation.
No benchmark set, no competitor or detection timings, a single 6-point experiment; the auditor standard is absent.

transferable: Encode l edge labels in binary across ceil(log2(l+1)) graph layers so vertex-colour-only automorphism tools can process coefficient-labelled graphs (Def. 2, eq. (2), p. 5).
Use a sparse four-array tensor (M, I, J, K) as the intermediate representation of a QCQP for structure detection (p. 4).
coauthors: Georgia Kouyialis (first; conceptualization with R.M., methodology), Xiaoyu Wang (validation); Misener supervision (p. 10)

quotes.text: Because dom(f) may be nonconvex and difficult to compute, this paper considers a GQCQP restriction that enforces symmetry on the entire box bounds

Although our strategies effectively convert the point packing QCQP into a mixed-integer linear optimization problems, we could have alternatively designed a branch-and-bound algorithm that is symmetry aware.

title: Efficient verification of relu-based neural networks via dependency analysis
contribution: Introduces dependency analysis between ReLU node states, turned into runtime dependency cuts inside a big-M MILP branch-and-bound, and the Venus tool combining it with input splitting, symbolic intervals and ideal cuts, which solves more ACAS Xu, MNIST and CIFAR-10 verification queries than Marabou, Neurify and NSVerify.
problem_entry: Safety-critical AI needs certification and no complete verifier scales to industrial networks; prior work reduces variables or tightens bounds, this paper reduces the branch-and-bound configuration space (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: Detect implications between stable states of unstable ReLU nodes (intra-layer via bounds on the zero-preactivation hyperplane, consecutive-layer suffices) relative to the current partial configuration and add them as dependency cuts through solver callbacks (Defs 1-2, Lemmas 1-3, Algorithm 1, pp. 3-5).
assumptions: Feed-forward ReLU networks; polyhedral input sets for MILP; big-M with precomputed bounds; only complete verifiers compared; tunable splitting discount, stability cut-off and callback frequency (pp. 2-3, 6, 8).
proof_devices: Counting: each dependency removes 2^(n-2) configurations, a factor 1/4 (p. 3)
Intra-layer dependency conditions from bounds on one node's pre-activation when the other's is zero (Lemma 1, p. 4)
Consecutive-layer dependencies imply all inter-layer ones (Lemma 2, p. 4); closed-form tests (Lemma 3, p. 4)
Cut validity: equivalent to the dependency on extensions of h, trivially satisfied otherwise (Thm 1, p. 5)
Procedure cost O(k s^2) (p. 5); proofs not included in the AAAI text
experiments: ACAS Xu (172 queries), MNIST 2x512 (eps 0.05, 100 images), CIFAR-10 1024-512-512 (eps 0.01, 100 images); vs Marabou, Neurify, NSVerify; 1 h per query, 24 h global, i7-7700K; solved count, total time, time on commonly solved, ratio to Venus (Table 1, p. 7); cactus plot (Fig. 4); MNIST ablation (Table 2); callback-frequency and radius sweeps (Figs 5-6, p. 8); per-benchmark parameters, analyser off on ACAS (p. 6); single runs.
positioning: Sorts literature into complete/incomplete and MILP/SMT/refinement; excludes incomplete methods as not comparable; builds on Anderson et al. ideal formulations and Wang et al. symbolic intervals; uses group's NSVerify as plain-MILP control (pp. 1-2, 5-6).
writing: Strong contribution claim ('at least one order of magnitude', 'Crucially, and differently'); hedged mechanism claims ('suggest'); sober conclusion that scalability will not be solved soon (pp. 1, 7-8).
limits_future: Dependency analysis cost needs callback-frequency tuning; slower counterexample generation than Neurify; splitting ineffective at high input dimension; degraded radii 0.05-0.07; future: transformational robustness (pp. 5, 7-8).

method_links.note: Dependencies between ReLU states are detected and exploited; conclusion that MILP solvers should not be used as black boxes.
Trained network written as MILP constraints (big-M plus ideal cuts) and its piecewise-linear structure exploited in branch-and-bound; precursor of the NN-as-constraints line leading to OMLT.
Components judged inside the full tool by ablation; dependency analyser switched off where it does not pay (ACAS); cut callbacks rationed.
Strong current competitors, plain-MILP control, cactus plot and written losses, but per-benchmark tuning of own tool, single runs, no independent check of returned counterexamples described.

new_pattern_candidates.pattern: optimization brought into a neighbouring AI formalism
new_pattern_candidates.evidence: MILP branch-and-bound structure exploitation carried into neural-network verification with a verification group (Lomuscio).

transferable: Derive pairwise implications between binary variables from interval bounds under a hyperplane restriction and add them as cuts valid for all extensions of the current node (Lemma 1, Def. 2, Thm 1, pp. 4-5).
Compute dependencies online relative to the solver's partial assignment, because offline most nodes are unstable (p. 4).
Choose split dimension by maximal average child stability ratio and stop with a depth-discounted score (pp. 5-6).
Report solved count, total time, time on the commonly solved core and a ratio column side by side (Table 1, p. 7).
Sweep the frequency of an expensive callback and report the U-shaped cost curve (Fig. 5, p. 8).
coauthors: Elena Botoeva, Panagiotis Kouvaros, Jan Kronqvist, Alessio Lomuscio (Imperial College London); alphabetical author order

quotes.text: This suggests that MILP solvers are not necessarily best used as black boxes, but application-specific considerations can help to improve their effectiveness.
The only aspect we found Venus to be less performing was counterexample generation where Neurify was the fastest tool.
